utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it please your Honours, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry and Mr. Turone, and Ms. Van Dusschoten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, together with my colleague Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Zejnil Olujic. I appear for Zdravko Mucic, together with my colleague Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Salih Karadzic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Hazim Delic, together with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, my name is John Ackerman and I am appearing here today for Mr. Esad Landzo, and my co-counsel is Ms. Cynthia McMurray.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber wishes to start these proceedings by giving our decision on the application to call additional witnesses. The Trial Chamber has carefully considered the Prosecution's written application for leave to call additional witnesses, the written response of the Defence for the accused Zejnil Delalic, and the contributions of all parties during the oral arguments on this issue. We have also considered the written response of the Defence for the accused Zejnil Delalic. We have decided to grant the Prosecution leave to call the additional witnesses identified in its application by the numbers one through to seven. It is clear from the arguments of the parties that the Prosecution's compliance with the disclosure obligations is the root of the contention. It is obvious that the final witness notification in the application, which is dated 4th July 1997, is four months later than the 7th March 1997 date fixed by the Trial Chamber in its Scheduling Order of 25th January 1997 for the Prosecution to disclose the names and other particulars of its witnesses to the Defence. Thus it is obvious that the Prosecution's compliance or otherwise with its disclosure obligations is called into question. But it is also clear that the Prosecution relied on the express words of Rule 67(A)(i), which allows it to notify the Defence of the names of the witnesses it intends to call in proof of the guilt of the accused and in rebuttal of any Defence plea of which the Prosecutor has received notice in accordance with sub rule (ii) below. The emphasis here is on the names of the witnesses that it intends to call in proof of the guilt of the accused. The witnesses involved in this case may be classified in two categories; witnesses one to five in one category and witnesses six and seven in another. Witnesses one to five: In a letter dated 5th December 1996, the Prosecution informed the Defence that barring agreement between the parties as to the authentication of certain documents, it would call additional witnesses for authentication purposes. On 13th May 1997, they gave notice of the names of these possible witnesses, namely witnesses one to five related to the issue of authentication. It is obvious that prior to the commencement of the present proceedings, the Prosecution had no intention of calling these five persons as witnesses, thus its sub-rule 67(A)(i) obligation to disclose their names and particulars to the Defence had not crystallised at the time it submitted its initial witness list on 7th March 1997. The Trial Chamber is satisfied, on a consideration of all the submissions of the Prosecution, that when the Prosecution did form the intention to call these witnesses, it informed the Defence on 13th May 1997 and sought leave of the Trial Chamber on 4th July 1997. It does not appear to the Trial Chamber that there has been any mala fides on the part of the Prosecution with respect to these witnesses. In respect of witnesses six and seven, again there does not appear to be any mala fides on the part of the Prosecution; in fact to the contrary it appears that the Prosecution has set out, in its application and its response to the Defence reply, a totally credible set of events which, taken together, rendered it unable to previously fulfil its disclosure obligations. Thus, the Prosecution's non-compliance with the Trial Chamber Scheduling Order is an insufficient ground on its own to deny the application to call any of these seven witnesses. There are, however, further considerations that have weighed on the Trial Chamber. As we are all aware, the Trial Chamber is charged with the duty under Article 20 of the International Tribunal's Statute of ensuring a fair trial for the accused persons. One of the basic indices of such a fair trial is the right of the accused to have adequate time for the preparation of his defence as prescribed in Article 21. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the Defence has had adequate time to prepare for these additional witnesses and as such, it will not be unduly prejudiced if the Prosecution calls them to give evidence. On 13th May 1997, over two and a half months ago, the Prosecution disclosed that it might call these witnesses. On 4th July, a month ago when it was sure that it will call the witnesses it put the Defence on notice and sought leave of the Trial Chamber. In the opinion of the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution has done what is required of it and the Defence has had adequate time to prepare for these witnesses. The Trial Chamber has taken note of the apprehensions of the Defence, particularly in relation to witnesses 6 and 7. With regard to these witnesses the Trial Chamber will give full consideration to convincing arguments supporting any measures requested of it in future in accordance with the fundamental principles of fairness. All participants in the present proceedings are urged to remember that the Trial Chamber is an instrument of justice to all concerned, not only to the accused persons, who without doubt have the most substantial interest in these proceedings, but also to the victims, the witnesses and the international community as a whole. In the pursuit of justice, the Trial Chamber has to consider all those lawful avenues through which a truthful picture of the events that surround the present proceedings may be made known. In deciding in favour of the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber has sought to balance all these interests, particularly the rights of the accused persons, the duties of the Prosecution and its role as an instrument of justice. As I said, this is our interim decision. I think this will enable us to clear the fog surrounding the calling of additional witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a -- I do not know how else to raise this but this way, if there is another way I am pleased to be advised of it. There is an error in the transcript that changes the meaning of the ruling you just entered, your Honour. It is on page 3, line 12, what appears in the transcript is "following argument" and the words that your Honour said were "barring agreement". This changes it quite dramatically. "Following argument" should be substituted with "barring agreement".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Prosecution, where do we stand with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness that the Prosecution intends to call notified me first thing this morning that he wanted certain protective measures in relation to himself in order for him to give his testimony. I might just say, your Honours, that this issue was raised with this witness on a number of occasions previously and up until this morning his position has been that he did not need or require protective measures, but since arriving at The Hague he has changed his mind in relation to it. Your Honours, I have questioned him about the situation, and it does not seem -- the issues that particularly concern him is publication outside of the chamber, so he is concerned about the image of his face being shown on television outside of the courtroom and so in that respect, he has asked me to make an application so that the image of his face can be distorted on the television outlet that leaves the building. The other matter that he has requested is that he did not want to have his name published in newspapers and the like. In relation to that, your Honour, that is perhaps a more difficult matter because his name, of course, has appeared publicly on witness lists and certainly no attempt has been made up to this stage to conceal that. I have spoken to him about the issue, and have covered with him the circumstances which cause him to give rise to requesting me to make this application. Your Honours, frankly this witness does not fall into the usual category of witness that would more readily justify the making of an order, especially the granting of a pseudonym, but I should say, your Honours, that he has presented himself as being a person under some considerable stress that I have observed since he has been here. He tells me your Honours -- he is 47 years of age, he tells me that he has since been -- since the war in 1992 he has had a heart attack, and he is at the moment experiencing chest pains, but he still nevertheless is willing to proceed. The position with respect to the medication he is on is a bit ambiguous. It seems he has been prescribed medication but he has not been taking it. He tells me he did see a doctor two weeks ago in relation to his chest pains and, as I said, he is currently at the very moment that I spoke to him before coming into the courtroom said that he is suffering from chest pains but he does not feel that the pains are sufficiently strong enough to prevent him from giving evidence, but he has asked me that if they get worse, can I raise the matter with the Chamber and I have undertaken to him that I would do that. Your Honours, I cannot make this application for the distortion of the image and the suppression of his name justifiably, I do not think, on the basis of any fears that he may have where he lives, but it would certainly, it seems to me, considerably relieve the stress that he is presently under in terms of giving his evidence now if he was to know that he was given these protective measures. I have not had an opportunity to raise this matter with the Defence. As I say, I found out about it this morning just after nine o'clock when I then went into a discussion with him about the matter. I do formally apply for it, your Honours, and I submit that if your Honours were inclined to grant these measures, I think it would considerably assist in the obtaining of the evidence that he is to present before the chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: My greatest fear in this is the impracticability of some aspects of the protective measures, because if everything about him is already known and is out, what is the use of a protective measure now, except that of distorting his image?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have brought that to his attention and I cannot but agree with your Honour. His name has been given to the Defence and I do not know how much further or wider it has been circulated about that. Certainly his image, as far as I am aware, has not been made public. I have spoken to him and asked him whether he has ever participated in interviews on television and the like and he tells me he has not. He says he has never spoken to any journalists or media people in relation to what evidence he would give before this chamber. To some extent, your Honours, I think there is perhaps still room for protective measures and that those measures could still have some effect so it would not as such be a totally empty order but I cannot but concede, your Honour, that if complete protection was sought to be offered then it is far too late to achieve that end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If we are to grant the application, we have to limit it to the possible aspects for which the order can be made. The question of distorting his image is the only thing that is outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I acknowledge that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you consider the order that this Trial Chamber can make.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think the facial distortion would go a long way, your Honour, to easing his concerns and I think he would understand, your Honour, the position but that is what he has asked me to do. I have raised the matter and I cannot put it any higher than the fact that he is a man who is under some stress. He is a man who would appear to be -- appear to have a medical condition which may in fact be exacerbated by public exposure of his name and identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the Defence view about the protection?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is true, as we have discussed several times so far, that each witness in accordance with Rule 69 under special circumstances may request protective measures. What I find strange is that speaking about this trial as a public trial, which should be accessible to all, to find ourselves in a situation to discuss protective measures just before the witness is due to appear in court, and I fear that this could become a habit, and we might believe the claims of the witnesses regarding the justification of protective measures as a principle. That is why I would oppose this kind of request for protective measures without, of course, interfering with the right of the witness to have such protective measures under special circumstances. The second point I should like to make is that my learned colleague the Prosecutor has indicated the reasons given by this witness. I do not know who could take upon themselves the risk of his physical condition, if it is true that this witness had a heart attack, and he still has chest pains and we do not have the view of a physician as regarding his capacity to testify, I fear that we could witness certain medical problems of this witness. It is true that this is just what the witness has said as the Prosecutor has informed us, but being laymen, one knows what chest pains mean for a heart patient. Regardless of this, I would like to appeal to you that our colleagues from the Prosecution, for the sake of the full realisation of the right to Defence and the preparation of the Defence, in addition to your efforts for them to disclose the whole list of witnesses, that they give us a precise list of witnesses for next week so that what happened yesterday should not happen again, and I am saying this only to take advantage of this opportunity I have been given to speak so as not to have to rise again. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, two points that I would like to make. First of all, I would like to commend my colleague Mr. Niemann on the very candid way that this matter was presented to the court this morning. Secondly, I am also concerned about the health of this witness. I also, and I think several of us here in the room, have some knowledge of what chest pains can mean. It seems to mean just out of an abundance of caution, your Honour, that this witness ought to be examined by a doctor, which could probably happen rather quickly, and have us advised. He probably has no idea the stress that might be involved with testimony in this room, and we could get some advice on whether his condition is such that he should not be subjected to that stress today, or whether he should be given some medication or something like that before we just run him in here and put him under that stress and take the risk of him falling out of his chair. None of us would want that to happen, none of us would want to take any responsibility for not having raised the matter and sought some way to assure ourselves before we do that with this man that he can testify safely in a healthy way. That is what I would suggest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I speak with some personal experience. Many years ago, I was cross-examining a defendant who had a heart attack in the dock. It is an extremely distressing experience for everybody when that happens. I would not want it to happen in this case. It affects the way in which one approaches a cross-examination of a witness. You are fearful if you get really stuck into it, he is going to have a heart attack. It is only fair to the Defence that we know precisely what this man's condition is, particularly as he appears to be negligent about taking his medicine, according to the Prosecution. I would support my learned friend Mr. Ackerman's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am grateful to the Defence for being so concerned about the health and condition of a Prosecution witness. If the Prosecution thinks that their witness might not be able to stand the risk of examination and cross-examination, I suppose they should tell us now, if you are confident or can see any reasons why he would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I find myself in agreement with what the Defence is saying here. I am in no position to make any judgment in terms of his medical condition, I can only relate to you what he has told me. I have no idea whether or not he is in a position to withstand cross-examination or evidence-in-chief or whatever. I do apprehend that we could perhaps have him medically examined very quickly and I could see the value in that. It certainly would, I think, make us all more at ease if we had a medical opinion to the effect that he was in fact in a position ready to enter the witness box and that his medical condition was such that he could do that. Certainly, your Honours, we have not had much of an opportunity to be with this witness, he arrived yesterday, and it was not expected he would have been called this week. Generally these things develop during the period of time the witnesses are here and medical attention and so forth can be rendered to them. But having regard to the very short period of time that he has been here, that opportunity has not presented itself, and indeed he did not inform us of that position, I understand, until -- he did not tell me at least until this morning and I understand he did not tell anyone in the Witness and Victims Unit until last night. It seems to me, your Honours, that we could probably have him medically examined by a doctor and I would endeavour to see if we could do that as expeditiously as possible and then if we did receive a green light, as it were, for him to go ahead then that may -- that would permit us to proceed today and it may also assist your Honours in making any determination with respect to the application I have made as well. I am in your Honours' hands. I can only report to your Honours that he has said to me that he is willing to proceed. He is in the witness room ready to go now, so that is the position I am in, but I am afraid I can give no advice on the question of his state of health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The possibility of offering protection is to keep the witness at ease as much as possible and to enable him to give his evidence, to absent all the other fears which he had before now. This appears to be a more precipitate one, where he is even having pains already. I think I would prefer him to be examined first before we will be able to determine whether we can take him, and I suppose an examination would enable the doctors to prescribe suitable medication which might carry him through. With the confidence that the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution is so interested in his health, perhaps much of his fears might be allayed and he might feel better to give evidence. I think we might rise for some time. Do you know how soon you will be able to get this done so we know when to come back? If you have a substitute witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am afraid we do not. Your Honours, we will undertake to keep both the Defence and your Honours' clerk notified about progress in this matter. If all goes well, hopefully we will be able to proceed this morning, late this morning some time, if we are able to get a medical practitioner to look at him in that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will rise and wait for the results. (10.35 am) (Adjourned until 2.30 pm) (2.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How do we stand with you, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Your Honours, the witness has now been examined by a Dutch medical practitioner, and the results of the examination are that the condition or pain that he was suffering this morning is not as a consequence of his heart at all, and that the doctor is of the opinion that there is no reason why he should not proceed to give his testimony in court and the doctor is of the opinion that there is no fear of any consequences so far as his heart is concerned from proceeding to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have spoken to the witness in light of the finding of the doctor and asked him whether he still wished me to pursue his request for protective measures. He still tells me that he does wish me to pursue that, but I have nothing further that I can add in relation to what I said this morning about that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We understand it and we can only give him the limited type of protection which his situation deserves. I think that is all we can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. Might I raise a matter with your Honours? If your Honours decide he should be referred to by a pseudonym, or have your Honours decided that his image should be distorted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I really do not see the value of a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is as I understood you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: His name has been advertised sufficiently if anyone wanted to know. BRANKO SUDAR (sworn) Examined by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the court has granted to you certain measures with respect to the distortion of the image of your face when it is broadcast on the television. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Branko Sudar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Cerici, Konjic on November 4th 1949.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend your education, did you receive your education in that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I completed my school there, I was a skilled driver and obtained my highly skilled driving qualifications there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ethnic background, I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where were you living at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was living in my house down at Cerici in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your employment at that time, at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was employed from 1968 with Sipad enterprise, Konjic, until the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sipad Enterprises, what is the nature of the work that that organisation carries on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forestry and timber and I myself was in the transportation department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sudar, could you move closer to the microphone please? You cannot be heard sitting back that far. Sir, can you tell me the ethnic background of the majority of the citizens who resided in the village of Cerici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority of the people living in Cerici were Serbs by nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am married.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In early 1992, did you have occasion to leave Cerici with your wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had occasion in the beginning of 1992, I felt the presence of some armies in Cerici. They came there, they killed. I noticed that something was very wrong, so I took my wife and children and transferred them to Montenegro. Then I returned home to Cerici, then I saw lots of unknown soldiers roaming through the city, HVO people in black uniforms and some others wearing some berets and fezes on their heads, unknown troops to me. Then I again tried to transfer my wife and children away to get them away, but I could not pass through the city because I was stopped so we came back home to Cerici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw these troops in and around Cerici, what time was that, about what period was that, in terms of the month of the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in April, at the beginning of April or thereabouts, I was in the city and I noticed these things, I noticed right away that something was wrong so I took the measures which I described to get my children and my wife away to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then return --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She joined her parents in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then return to Cerici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I then returned to Cerici and I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May 1992, did you observe certain military activities going on in and around the town of Cerici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Cerici, I was there -- a neighbour of mine Vlado Draganic went to town and he was locked up somewhere in town in a motel and was beaten up there. He returned all black and blue home and then I thought to myself that things were really hard and I had to do something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at home on 20th May in my garden, watering the peppers. I heard some shots, then I saw some army, some soldiers exercising on the sports ground and I went up to my old man, to his house, to see what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise who these forces were that you saw exercising on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore all sorts of uniforms, how shall I describe them? To tell you the truth, I did not dare go to the town, but those people who had seen them from close say they were some unknown troops there and we did not dare go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the next thing to happen to you in relation to this military activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And another thing, we were in Cerici with my father and my mother and I saw people from Bjelasnica which is another village near to Cerici and from another place called Sudar Potok they also escaped to Cerici. All the villagers from those surrounding villages had fled to Cerici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these people appeared to be refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were mostly refugees, they were fleeing from their homes. Everybody was fleeing to this creek to hide to get away from the bullets and from the unknown troops that had attacked from the city. I do not know who they were, but mostly they wore berets, people from Bjelasnica were also attacked and from that direction, so that all the people had to flee, to hide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the attack go on for, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attack went on somewhere from 20th May it started and 21st there was shelling and I heard that Jovo Gotovac had been killed in the shelling, also Uros Djurica or rather Djurica Uros was wounded and somebody transferred him into town and he died there, I do not know the details. So women and children started crying and they were fearful and in the meantime, Rajko Cecez, Mirko Cecez and Slobodan Draganic called up the President of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you there when the call was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there, I was outside because the only telephone that was working was at my father's, because before the attack all the lines of the Serbs had been cut and there was no communication and this was the only telephone that was still working. Why and how I really do not know. Then they called up the President of the municipality, they spoke to him nicely. They said that the people were not to blame, that the attacks should stop and the man promised, and there was no more shooting. They said that we should go down to the river to Ugostica and come to some kind of an agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then proceed to go down to the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 22nd May, we gathered there, there were about 20 of us from Cerici, my neighbours, there were two or three people from about Bjelasnica. We crossed the bridge at the river and we thought that the President of the municipality would come there as he had promised. In the meantime, people ran out of the woods shouting "hands up" and to which all had to raise up our hands, they started beating us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we just stop for a moment. Just slow down, if you could, for me, Mr. Sudar, please this all has to be translated. If you could just take it a little bit more slowly, please. When you were told to go down to the river with that group of people, were you also given any instructions with respect to anything that you had to take with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the President said very nicely "anyone who has any weapons should carry them along and bring them there", and the people who had anything, they did bring those weapons along. However, they took them away. They took our belts and coats and whatever we had on and then they started beating us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that took these things away from you, did you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, because -- I think his first name is Masic, he is the one who took my purse, my driving licence, I had 200 marks and the last salary I had received in my company, he took all that away from me, he took off my belt and anything else I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This gentleman by the name of Masic, do you know his ethnic background, the one that took the things away from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is by nationality a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said apart from having the things taken off you, you were also beaten. Do you know who it was that beat you at that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Macic, he had gloves on his hands, like some kind of special boxing gloves, and they beat us with rifles, with whatever they could get their hands on, people were dropping from the blows, falling down on the sand, on the rails, some people lost consciousness and when we came to, we all had to get up again and then in the direction of Celebici, the military facility there, we had to go across the bridge with two or three guards and we had to go in front of them up to that military facility and the tunnel there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is it approximately from that place by the river where you surrendered and the camp at Celebici? What is the distance from the bridge where you were beaten to the camp at Celebici, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly I think it can be about three kilometres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get from the bridge to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the bridge to Celebici we reached the gates where the camp was on foot, we went on foot, with two or three of these soldiers of theirs who had their guns pointed at us and they led us to that spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately, if you can remember, how many soldiers were involved in capturing you and the people that were with you that went to that bridge site on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, the attack came from all around, from Konjic, from the other side, from Bjelasnica, from Pokojiste and there were even snipers used. My house was under fire, you could not escape the snipers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you were able to observe of the attack on Cerici, did you see anybody returning fire from the town out of Cerici towards the people who were attacking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not notice anything because Vros Djurica and I, we were in the village, Slobodan Draganic also, there was firing at about Bjelasnica, at Donje Selo, that is 2.5 or 3 kilometres away from me, so we could not see anything. I really cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know whether or not the Serb military forces were anywhere in the vicinity at the time of this attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In our opinion, there were no Serb military forces. There may have been about 30 people in Cerici and some people had fled from about Bjelasnica. According to them, about 2,000 of them had attacked but even if we had defended ourself, there would not have been more than 150 of us able bodied men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the 150 able bodied men that you have spoken of, were any of them engaged in defending the village of Cerici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not. Everybody was fleeing, all the population of about Bjelasnica, Donje Selo fled down to the stream, so I really cannot give you any better answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago in your evidence how you were taken some 2 to 3 kilometres from the bridge to the military camp at Celebici. Can you tell the court what happened when you arrived at the camp at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived at the Celebici camp, we passed the entrance to the gates and then we all had to line up against the wall to put our hands behind our heads and our group consisted of some 20 men. We stood there, there were some women up there too and some children, they were crying out "kill the Chetniks, what are you doing with them, beat them". Then they beat us, we fell down from the blows, we would fall on the concrete, then we would have to get up again almost until the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court approximately what time it was in the day when you arrived at the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was about 1 or 2 o'clock, I really cannot remember exactly, but it was afternoon, between noon and 3 pm. I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people that were administering these beatings to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time there was some young men that I could not really recognise. They were calling out somebody by the name of Sok. We did not dare turn around, we were facing the wall. We did not know what was hitting you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what you were being beaten with on that occasion when you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With rifles, with planks, with shovels, with all kinds of things. As far as I could see there were some baseball bats, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this beating had taken place, what happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we had been beaten up, we were taken to the hangar. I later learnt it was called number 22. It was about 5 or 6 metres wide, 10 or so long, I cannot tell exactly because I really did not see it properly. I really cannot estimate the size, so we entered the hangar number 22. When we entered we saw somebody who had worked in the court, Danilo Zivak sitting in the corner, there were some other men there but I cannot remember their names. I saw Babic Slobodan, he was on the floor with his hands up. He was covered in blood, he was not quite conscious and then we spent the time there until evening and when night fell. They started to blindfold us and two of them would take each one of us somewhere, to some kind of a court. You had to make some kind of a statement with your eyes tied. They would beat us, hit us, so all 20 of us had to go to this some kind of a judge blindfolded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were beaten. Were you beaten at the time when you were interrogated, or were you beaten either going to or coming from it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, I think I was beaten -- I know they hit me in the eye, I cannot remember exactly, but my eye was closed. I could not see, I could not see for 20 days through that eye. I cannot remember all the details. After all, five years has gone by, but I think it was when we were going out, as far as I can remember, but I cannot be 100 per cent sure, but I know somewhere around the doors that they beat me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were interrogated, what was it they were asking you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked us whether we were Serbs, whether we were members of the SDS, all kinds of things, where we came from, what our names were, what we had, all kinds of questions they were asking. So you really do not even know what they are asking because we were all in some kind of a state of shock and we suffered from the beating. Then two men would take you there to the judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I may have asked you this question, but can you tell us the date it was that you first went to Celebici camp, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to the Celebici camp on 22nd May, and then we stayed there until about 10 or 11 at night and we were beaten. Two of them may have stayed behind. Then I heard from somebody they were saying: "Pavo Mucic is coming so do not beat them any more", so they did not beat the last two. In the meantime they said half of us should get ready to go to Musala, Konjic. Half of them left, then I stayed behind. Then when the van came a second time, the rest of us got in and we were driven to the sports hall in Konjic known as Musala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who it was that said that you would be going, to prepare yourself to go to the Musala sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly now. I really cannot remember who said it. Somebody said it outside and in all that pain and suffering, some people were dragging their feet, we climbed up. We did not even know where we were going or how we were going. We did not really know what was happening to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you arrive at the Musala sports hall that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived that night in the sports hall. We found some people there too. How they got there I do not know. They threw us into the cloakrooms, the locker rooms where children change for gym, and we slept in class rooms about 22, 24 of us, and the room was something like 2.5 by 4 metres. There were one or two chairs and we all lay on the floor. Then for about two or three days they did not give us any food, then later on they would give us a piece of bread. Also they hardly gave us any water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who "they" are? You keep referring to "they". Who was it who did not give you any food and kept you locked up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am thinking of the soldiers, the soldiers who had beaten us. I assumed -- I saw a taxi driver there, Habibija they called him. Then there was Jeleskovic, he was there too, I think they called him Muf, then Halic -- they were Muslims, predominantly Muslims. There were one or two Croats, I do not know their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the sports hall, Musala sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there for about 20 days. Again, I cannot remember exactly the number of days. In the meantime, one evening towards night fall, Hazim Delic came, told me to get up, asked me where I came from. Actually he called out five or six of us, "get ready", he said, and we did and we climbed on to a van without knowing where we were going. Then he sat there with the driver, there was another one with him. They took us to Celebici. Afterwards I realised that it was a camp and they put us in the hangar known as number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Hazim Delic came. Did he call you out --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Hazim Delic, not Delalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I said that, I am sorry. I certainly meant to say Hazim Delic. You said Hazim Delic called out the names. Did he call out your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He called out my name and a group of five or six of us, we had to get into the van and he took us to Celebici. When I got to Celebici, they threw us into the hangar on the concrete floor, I was placed near the door. He said "lie there".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said lie there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic when he brought me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the hangar, did you know what number hangar that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They called it number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person Hazim Delic, had you ever seen or met this person before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Hazim Delic, I worked with him. I never had any problems with him, I really do not know what happened. We never had any quarrels or disputes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you worked with Hazim Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in this enterprise since 1968. He came later. I think we must have worked together for more than 10 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Sipad Enterprises, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sipad Prenj Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that Mr. Delic worked there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you see him at work from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From time to time I would see him at work, but more recently just before this war, I do not know maybe he took unpaid leave, but I did not see him for two or three months. Where he went, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is two or three months before the war started in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think the end of 1991 and beginning of 1992, something like that, during the winter, that winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what sort of work Mr. Delic used to do when he was at the factory -- at the business that you worked at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic, in Sipad Prenj, he was a metal worker. He worked in the transport department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any members of Mr. Delic's family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, I know his father, his wife. I just do not know his children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his father's name, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His father's name is Ibro, he worked in the carpentry, in the building enterprise. I would see this man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same business for whom you worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was called the Nerveta company, then he was transferred, I think, to a company called Izgradnja Construction Work, but I would see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the village that Hazim Delic came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He lived in Orahovica, a neighbouring village across the lake from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how far is that village from Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about four to five kilometres, about five, something like that. That is my estimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, apart from working in the same business that you worked for, do you know whether Mr. Delic had any private businesses that he was running at the time; this is prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His father or he or his sister, they had opened some kind of a shop, a souvenir shop in town. They were selling something, books or something like that. I did not go to that shop actually. I would pass by, I never entered it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going back to the time when you say Mr. Delic put you into hangar number 6, when you went into that hangar was there anyone inside the hangar at the time when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I entered the hangar there were about 250 to 300 people, something like that, at least 250, I think. I was sitting just next to the door, in the second line from the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay in this place, the second line -- did you stay in this same place in the second line for the whole period of time that you were in Celebici camp, or did you move from place to place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not move. Where they put me, I stayed there all the time until I was transferred again, and I went to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what the conditions were like inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions in the hangar were terrible. We all slept on the concrete floor. The food, one day there would be some, the next there would not. When bread arrived, a loaf would be cut up into 15, 16 even 17 slices and we would get a slice in the morning and at night. They would give us a spoonful of water, a ladleful. Also the door was kept shut, there was no air, we were so crammed we could not breath. It was impossible to live under those conditions. Then the toilet; at night, there was some kind of a bucket that we had to use for those purposes. In the daytime we would go out. There was a kind of hole behind the hangar and when they felt like it they would let us use it, so that as far as the hangar is concerned. It was awful. It was dirty. There was dust. Later some people fell ill, somebody called Jovak, then there were lice. Zenga would take a dog and walk around with this dog, he and Osman Dedic. I do not know all the surnames of these guards. I just know some of the first names. They would take a dog, but fortunately the dog did not jump on us, nor did he bite us, but that is what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that sometimes you were allowed to leave the hangar to go to a toilet outside during the day. Were there times when you were prevented from going to the toilet outside during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes we were prohibited, so we had to do our best without and when we went to pee then there would be 10 to 15 of us in a line. Delic would come and he would order us to form a line "go to urinate". Then we would go and then we would have to come back, we would have to run back. Sometimes people did not even have time to do it and the time was very limited. He would rush us. But sometimes they would let us go of our own, just behind the hangar, the guards were there. There was also a trench there, sometimes we would be taken to the trench.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people ever beaten or interfered with when they went to the toilet by the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards beat us to tell you the truth. They beat us -- it depended. Sometimes somebody would go out and get hit, someone else would not get hit. It all depended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the place where you were seated in the hangar, where were you in relation to the doorway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was close to the doorway, facing it with my back, but sometimes I could look around because mostly we had to sit with our hands on our knees crouching. That is how we had to sit. When anyone appeared we had to bend our heads down and sit in that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the door of the hangar was opened, were you able to see outside and see what was happening outside during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the door was open I could see the guards, the troops passing by, soldiers passing by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the door was closed was it possible for you to hear sounds outside of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the door was closed, every blow or when someone was taken out, we could hear everything. It is easy to hear the beating, the cries, the screams, the pleas for mercy. You could hear the voices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now want you to have a look at this model that appears in front of you and I would ask you to get up from your seat, but just wait until I give you the instructions because you have to have the headphones. I would ask you to rise from your seat -- you need to make sure that you stay behind the screen when you stand up and walk round, but I would like you to walk round the front of the model, look at it closely if you would and see if you can identify it and tell me where it is in that model, if you can, that hangar number 9 was -- hangar number 6 was that you were detained in. Perhaps if you just stand behind it, I understand you cannot walk around without being seen. If you can identify it from that position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is number 6 (indicates) the first building here, the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we will have to make do with that, because you cannot walk to the front apparently. During the time that you were detained in Celebici camp, did you lose any weight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lost about 35 to 30 -- 25 to 30 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke earlier of Mr. Hazim Delic, and you were able to tell me some particulars about him and about his family. Did you come to find out what position he held in the camp at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I heard from what the guards were saying, Delic was the deputy warden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the guards treat him in terms of their relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sometimes he criticised severely the guards and shouted at them just as he shouted at us, and then we noticed when Pavo was absent, he was the one in charge, the one who gave the orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Pavo. Is that some sort of a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is his nickname as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say his nickname, who do you mean by him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo -- I mean Mucic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Mucic before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know him before the war. I was in a village visiting a colleague of mine, also a driver and that is when I saw him once. We had coffee. Before that, I might have seen him, but I had no contact with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I use the word "know", what I am asking you is had you ever had occasion to meet him or see him prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prior to the war, as I said, I occasionally saw him in the street, but we did not "meet". He worked elsewhere and I only stayed at Igman seldom. I might have seen him, I saw him occasionally. I did not know what his name was. I only learnt later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you learn later what his name was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was with the Montenegran he introduced himself as Mucic and that is how I learnt of his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us some details about this meeting that you had with the Montenegran and how it is that you met Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came to this village, we met there and we were there together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Montenegran that you have referred to, was he in any way related or connected to Mr. Mucic so far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This Montenegran was a colleague of mine, and another taxi driver, also a Montenegran, came and I learnt that he was Pavo's brother-in-law, that Olga, Pavo's sister, was married to him and I learnt then that they called him Pavo, and that is when I got introduced to him. I did not know. I had not known him before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "introduced to him", who do you mean? Introduced to who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I actually mean, I was sitting there and he came there and then he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is he, could you tell us the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zdravko Mucic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately, you may not remember very precisely, but approximately either the year that this meeting took place, or if you cannot tell us that, can you tell us approximately how many years before the war it was that you met Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was somewhere around half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of the family members or people related to Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They lived in the city, I had heard about Janko, his brother, that he was also working at Igman, but I had virtually no contacts with him. I only had heard that he had a brother by the name of Janko and a father. I did not have much contact. Once I took timber up and there was a house of a Muslim and someone showed it to me and told me "this is Janko". That is all I know, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they lived in the city, what city are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Above the military installation, military factory at Igman, that section of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where Mr. Mucic worked just prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was in Austria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what position Mr. Mucic had at the camp? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How shall I put it? He used to come and when he came they would say that he was the warden. I do not know what his function was, but they would say "here comes the warden, here comes the commander". So I saw him three or four times coming to the entrance, and once he called out some names of people to be transferred from hangar number 6 to the sports hall, but while he was there, whenever we saw him, we were not exactly maltreated. We were not taken out to be beaten, at least while I was there, but mostly when he was not there, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Mucic enter hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he would enter the hangar. He would come on a motorbike, but when he was there, when he came we were not maltreated and soldiers would come inside. All sorts of soldiers and troops would come inside, they would come to the door, take a walk, return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of the other guards that were working in the Celebici camp during the time that you were being detained in hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for other guards, to tell you the truth, I did not know them. Zenga was there, but I did not know him. I might have seen him before as a child, but I did not know him. There was Osman, Kemo, there was a certain Focak, a policeman, there was a man from Bjela who I knew but I have now forgotten his name, he only came later. It eludes me, I cannot recall it right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person you referred to as Zenga, did you know what his surname was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Surname is Landzo, they called him Zenga and Landzo. I do not exactly know what his first name is. I am not sure of the first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of Mr. Landzo or members of his family prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew more of his family than of him. I knew his father but I was not in much contact with him. I knew his relatives, some of them were working in the saw mill and two of his father's brothers in Sipad in the timber at the present time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any members of his family, his father's brothers, anyone like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know his uncle Omer, I believe as far as I can recall that Omer is his name. I have forgotten all these things, I used to know them all. I have forgotten a lot. Nurko is his name, he worked at a saw mill, one of the uncles, he worked at the saw mill, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything about Zenga that you can recall as something that you could identify him by when he was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I do not know by what, by his appearance, he was small built. He was not tall, so-so. He had a thin voice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say a thin voice, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: High pitched voice when he shouted at us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you treated in the camp by Hazim Delic and Zenga Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hazim Delic would provoke me, ask me questions, where I worked, how had I worked, where did I come from. He would take me out then hit me and then afterwards he would give me a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landzo also once -- when I asked to go outside to the latrine he hit me in front of the door, he would not let me go and eventually when he did let me go, when I returned he hit me with a baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were being detained inside hangar number 6, did you know of a prisoner by the name of Scepo Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Scepo Gotovac, yes, I knew this elderly man from about Bjelasnica. He sometimes lived in town and sometimes in about Bjelasnica. He came, he was brought, once he stood by the door. That day Delic came he had a note in his hand and he asked who is Scepo Gotovac. The man answered "I am" and he said to him, "get up". When the man got up he hit him several times, five or six perhaps. I cannot remember exactly, but I do know that he hit him several times. The man fell down and starting crying out. Then they took him out. They continued to beat him. I could hear Zenga's voice. It was Zenga actually who called him out and then I could also subsequently hear his voice. Then we heard some water being poured on him, then they threw him inside through the door, wet as he was. I do not remember exactly who it had been, Zivak or somebody else who had to pull him inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were you referring to when you said "they took him out", that you could recognise their voices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, Zenga and Delic took him out. Delic was there, he called him out. He told him to come out and then Zenga, and Zenga's voice could be heard then, and also when he was being beaten, Zenga was shouting at him "how many Muslims have you killed", and Delic told Scepo Gotovac that as a Chetnik he had killed two Muslims in the war before that. They ask him again "how many did you kill" and he screamed and cried out for mercy, calling his mother's name and he was in terrible suffering. They beat him, again Zenga took him out again and beat him again. We could hear his voice. They would shut the door when they beat someone. You could only hear the voices outside. Then they threw him inside again. Afterwards in the morning he actually succumbed and you could hear no more cries, no more screams. He was silent and somebody said "Scepo is dead" and I did not want to look because I could never look at a dead man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What condition was he in when they returned him to the hangar after the beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How to put it -- he just lay there crumpled on the floor, crumpled and screaming, crying, moaning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything about his head at the time when he was returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga had hit him in the head. To tell you the truth, I did not like to look. I just could not bring myself to look at a dead man, but there was something wrong with his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say he succumbed the next morning. Did you actually look at him the next morning at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I told you, to tell you the truth I just could not bring myself to look at him. Some people took him out. I was unable to bring myself to cover him. I think some other people covered him a bit. I could not bring myself to look at the dead man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any stage look at him? You say he was a dead man, how did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He just lay there, he stopped moaning, and there were no signs or any sounds coming from him, so I concluded that he was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to do assist the court by telling us approximately the age, approximately the age of Scepo Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not quite sure, I think that he was born somewhere in 1920, I am not quite sure, perhaps he was a bit older than that, but I think so, about 1920 was the year in which he was born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what ethnic group Scepo Gotovac was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Scepo was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again during the period of time that you were detained in hangar number 6, did you know of a prisoner by the name of Simo Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard of Simo Jovanovic, he was some kind of a director. He had a fish pond up there at Njeba. We were not exactly very close, I had only heard of the man. He lay from across from where I was lying, leaning against a wall, they also took him out many times. There were also some neighbours of his there who would tell him "would you like some fish" and I am not sure, I do not know all these men. I only knew and heard that they were his neighbours and it was them who took him out repeatedly and beat him. The last several times they also poured water on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say these neighbours took him out, were these neighbours guards in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga and Cosic and some other guys and Subasic, I just now remembered, I found out their names later. I really did not know them well, they are younger men. I only learnt later it was them who had called out to him "would you like some fish" and when they did that, they also beat him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you hear what was happening to him outside of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard Zenga's voice outside the hangar. I saw him and other voices shouting -- you can hear the sound of beating. You can hear the sound of a stick landing on a body, and I really had to put my fingers in my ears not to hear that and not to hear the water hose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last time that Mr. Jovanovic was taken out and beaten, can you recall approximately how long this beating lasted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would take him out for 20 minutes at a time or 15 minutes, I cannot exactly recall how many minutes they would keep him outside, but they would keep beating him until he fainted and then they would just throw him inside in that condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the last occasion he was taken out, did you see who it was that returned him to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly and I cannot say if I cannot recall exactly. I think he was only actually pushed inside through the door and I could hear the voices outside. I could not see exactly. Then you were not allowed to look towards the door when it opened because you would also get hit if you looked at the door. If you could just furtively glance at the door you could see who it was, but you could not always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you could only hear what was going on outside. Did you recognise any of the voices on this last occasion that Mr. Jovanovic was beaten, of the guards that were outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard Zenga's voice and I could hear Delic was giving the orders and I could hear his voice out there. Sometimes he would say "enough, stop".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say sometimes he would say "enough, stop", who was saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard Delic say it twice or three times, "enough, stop, enough. No more".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the last occasion when he was brought into the hangar and left somewhere near the door, can you recall what condition he was in this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was totally beaten up and he was crying out for his mother and moaning in pain, and then his voice left him and he just huddled, crumpling in a corner. I do not know how to describe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did he stay at that place in that condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly, I believe that in the morning when he died, he was taken out. I cannot recall all the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that he died in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that he died in the morning, but I do know that he was dead. I cannot exactly remember, they were mostly -- they would mostly die in the night. I cannot recall all the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took him out the next morning, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga called him out and took him out, and the guys were still standing there, Osman and Kemo, and all the others. I could not watch the people who were beating him. I could only hear the voices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am referring to the next morning with they came. Did you see who it was that took him out of the hangar the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga called him out, as far as I could conclude. I cannot remember -- he could not walk on his own and people had to take him out, but I cannot remember that detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the last occasion that he was taken out, did you ever see him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw him again. He was never inside again, nor did he give any signs, nor did he scream.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he did not give any signs, he did not scream" did you see him in the condition when he did not give any signs or did not scream? Did you see him in that condition yourself, or is that something someone may have told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I cannot bring myself to look at a dead man and I tried not to look at them as they lay there by the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But difficult as it is for you to look, did you occasionally just glance across the room and look at the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Occasionally I would cast a glance and see him lying there, but there were no sounds or moans coming from that direction and I assessed from that, as the screams had stopped and the signs of life had stopped, that he was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also while you were detained in hangar number 6, did you ever come to know a prisoner by the name of Bosko Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosko Samoukovic, you mean. I knew this elderly man by sight, he is from Bradina. He was fourth in the row from the door next to the wall, there he stood with his son. I believe his name was indeed Elko, I am not sure of that. They stood there, then Zenga came in brandishing a pole or a stick, I cannot remember exactly. He started hitting the people in the line. First he hit Mrkajic, then he hit all the people standing in the line and the son of this old man and the old man, Bosko, many times and the man fell down. Then he ordered someone, I cannot remember exactly whom, take him out, lead him out and they led him out. Whether they gave him any aid I do not know. They took him to number 22. Someone came a bit later and said that he had died. He had been taken to number 22. He either died on the way to 22 or in the ward, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the beating first commenced, did that take place in hangar number 6, inside hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The beating took place precisely in hangar number 6. First they started beating Rajko Mrkajic and then the whole row of people. This was an elderly man, when he fell down and it was obvious he was about to die, then they ceased beating him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say this was an elderly man. Tell us who you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am referring to Bosko Samoukovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he was an elderly man, approximately how old was Bosko Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose that he was around 60, I am not quite sure of his exact age. I suppose that this was about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now break. We will come back at 4.30. (4.00 pm) (A short break) (4.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Shall we continue, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. So you were telling their honours about things that you had observed with respect to Mr. Bosko Samoukovic and you were in the middle of telling us about that at the adjournment. Can you tell their honours whether or not you know what this gentleman's ethnic background was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Serb, he was a Serb; Bosko Samoukovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you observed the beating that took place, when it first started, how far were you sitting away from this gentleman? Are you able to estimate that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe less than 10 metres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your evidence that you saw him being beaten, among others, by Zenga. Did you see what he was being beaten with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, he had a wooden plank, a board, a stick, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it that had the plank, just help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga had the plank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually observe Zenga hit Mr. Samoukovic with the plank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He beat everyone, the whole row, and he beat Samoukovic and the man fell from the blows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him when he fell from the blows, that is Samoukovic, what did they do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he also said something to the effect "take them away" as far as I can remember. They tried to give him some kind of aid and then they carried him away. I cannot remember all the details clearly, but I remember the beating and when the man fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, during the period of time that you were being detained inside hangar 6, did you know a prisoner by the name of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything happen to him during the time that he was in hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga would take him out, he would beat him inside too. He would take him out and he would cry out and scream and his -- he was holding on to his hands because he had burned him with something, I do not know what it was, but on his palms and his tongue as far as I can remember, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he had burned him with something, who are you referring to as "he"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga, Zenga had burned him, one could hear his voice, this was outside mostly and also inside, but I cannot recall the exact details, but inside, too, he would touch him and burn him. He was maybe 15 metres away from me. He was moaning and crying out. I cannot exactly say how it happened, but he was screaming and yelling and something was being done to him, and I saw the burns afterwards on his palms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you particularly when you were seeing things that were happening inside the hangar, did you see with what (redacted) was being burned with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could see, he was holding something like a knife as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to explain how it was that he was burnt with a knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He heated the knife and then with the red hot knife he would put it on his palms and you could see that all his palms were burnt from this red hot object.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he heat the knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how he heated it, maybe -- I think it was some gun powder, something yellow. He would set light to it and it would burn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
